newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean conglomerates join hands against takeovers.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean conglomerates join hands against takeovers.

text.p: In a clear warning to South Korea's first major corporate raider, a powerful industry group said on Tuesday that it opposed hostile takeovers and might intervene in such bids.
"We have to actively defend against any hostile takeover bid," Sohn Byung-doo, a senior official with the Federation of Korean Industries, told reporters.
"Federation members must help each other."
He was commenting on a possible takeover bid by Shindongbang Corp for Midopa Department Store Co, which has startled the stock market.
Takeovers are virtually unheard of in South Korea, although new rules that came into effect in January make them possible.
The federation represents the interests of major South Korean conglomerates, known as chaebol.
"We urge the two companies to compromise and are watching developments. If they fail, we plan to intervene to settle the issue," Sohn added.

Midopa became the target of the country's first hostile takeover bid when Shindongbang and Korea Industrial Co told the Korea Stock Exchange last Thursday they were considering taking over the retailer.
A senior executive with Shindongbang, the nation's largest edible oil company, shrugged off the federation's comments and said they would not alter the company's strategy.
"I don't believe Korean entrepreneurs will intervene in transactions between companies as they are men of sense and responsibility," said company director Kim Jin-il.
On Monday Shindongbang said it had bought a combined 6.74 percent stake in Midopa with joint venture Dongbang Peregrine Securities and aimed to participate in management.
"But this doesn't mean we have finally decided on a takeover bid," Kim said.
The federation warning drove Midopa's shares limit down for the second day running. The stock closed eight percent lower at 32,400 won ($37.05).
Takeover bid rumours had sent Midopa's share price rocketing from a year low of 16,300 won to 47,500 last week.
"Shindongbang is unlikely to fight against all the chaebol," said Ha Sung-won, a broker with Ssangyong Securities. "Midopa takeover talk is fizzling out."
Midopa operates a flagship store in Seoul's most fashionable shopping district and has 20 distribution outlets throughout South Korea.
Analysts said the federation's veiled threat could open it to criticism.
The government lifted a 10 percent limit on individual holdings in listed companies this year and is planning further liberalisation to allow mergers and acquisitions.
"It's very rare for the federation to speak up loudly about a specific issue," said Lee Hahn-koo, president of Daewoo Research and Economic Institute.
"It seems reluctant to abandon an old concept that mergers and acquisitions are unethical."
But Kim Joo-hyung, director of LG Research and Economic Institute, said he did not believe the federation intended to battle all takeover attempts.
"It reflects public suspicion that there is something morally wrong in this case," Kim said.
